_comment: Verified law backing every legal claim in the content bank. Every citation below was independently checked against primary/secondary sources on 2026-07-18, not merely copied from a prior draft. Nothing here should be repeated in marketing copy unless it traces back to one of these entries.
_phantomLawGuardrail: There is no Nevada 'October 1 deadline' for AI disclosure.
There is no 'Nevada AI fine' of $5,000 per interaction.
Nevada's comprehensive AI bill (SB 199) did not pass / died in committee.
The FCC's 'one-to-one consent' TCPA rule never took effect — do not describe it as live law or as something that 'took effect' in January 2026.

verifiedFacts: Statutory damages: $500 per negligent violation, up to $1,500 per willful/knowing violation.
No cap on aggregate class-action exposure — damages are per-violation.
The pre-2023 prior-express-written-consent (PEWC) standard governs marketing texts to cell numbers.

spine.topic: TCPA — one-to-one consent rule (VACATED, not live law)
citations: Insurance Marketing Coalition Ltd. v. FCC, No. 24-10277 (11th Cir., decided Jan. 24, 2025)
verifiedFacts: The FCC's 2023 'one-to-one consent' rule (consent to one entity at a time; logically-and-topically-related calls only) was vacated by the Eleventh Circuit on Jan. 24, 2025, three days before its scheduled effective date.
The rule never took effect. The FCC subsequently deleted the vacated language and reinstated the prior rule text.
Do not say the rule 'took effect' or describe a 'January 2026' compliance deadline for it.
What remains live: the older PEWC standard, and the fact that shared/resold 'up to N companies' lead consent is exactly what plaintiffs' attorneys target under that standard.
10DLC carrier registration for A2P text traffic remains a separate, live requirement enforced by carriers, not the FCC rule above.

citations: NRS 200.620 (interception/recording of wire communications; all-party consent)
NRS 200.650 (surreptitious recording of private in-person conversations; one-party consent)
Lane v. Allstate Ins. Co., 969 P.2d 938 (Nev. 1998)
verifiedFacts: Nevada is a hybrid-consent state: ALL-party consent for phone/wire calls (NRS 200.620); ONE-party consent for in-person conversations where the recorder is a participant (NRS 200.650).
Lane v. Allstate (1998) established that NRS 200.620 applies to any person recording their own telephone conversation without the other party's consent — no exception for private parties.
Sharpe v. State (2015) extended NRS 200.620's 'wire communication' to cellular calls and text messages, not just landline calls.
Violations are a category D felony under NRS 193.130: 1–4 years imprisonment, plus a fine of up to $5,000.
Do not describe this as a 'physical-location test' — the operative question is consent of all parties to the communication, not where anyone is standing.
Notice must be made 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay,' subject to law-enforcement needs and the time needed to determine scope/restore system integrity.
There is NO fixed hour or day count (e.g. no '72-hour' rule) in Nevada law. 72 hours is a GDPR (EU) requirement, not Nevada's.
If notification is required to more than 1,000 persons at once, nationwide consumer reporting agencies must also be notified without unreasonable delay.

spine.topic: Nevada — data security / payment card data
citations: NRS 603A.215 (payment card data; PCI DSS compliance; encryption)
verifiedFacts: A business that accepts payment cards must comply with the current PCI Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) as adopted by the PCI Security Standards Council.
For personal information not covered by PCI DSS, businesses may not transmit it electronically outside a secure system without encryption meeting recognized standards (e.g. NIST guidance).
Section 5 prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce, which the FTC has applied to AI systems that misrepresent themselves as human or misrepresent their capabilities.
This is a live, current federal standard — not a pending or proposed rule.
